title: Hasan's peace
hookLine: Hasan makes a treaty with Mu'awiyah to stop the bloodshed, as the Prophet ﷺ foretold (Bukhari)

lines: THIS SON OF MINE IS A LEADER.
cards: A boy sits beside his grandfather on the pulpit in Medina. The grandfather is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.

He looks out at the people, then at the boy, then at the people again, and says: this son of mine is a sayyid, a leader, and perhaps through him God will make peace between two great groups of Muslims.
Bukhari keeps the scene. The boy is Hasan, Ali's elder son. Years later, after his father's death, Hasan stands at the head of an army facing another army.

teach.b: Bukhari keeps the second scene too, in the words of a later narrator, al-Hasan al-Basri. Hasan leads armies he describes as like mountains. Facing him are the forces of Mu'awiyah, the governor of Syria.
One of Mu'awiyah's advisers says these armies will not turn back until each has destroyed the other.

teach.h: WHO WILL BE LEFT TO CARE FOR THE PEOPLE?
teach.b: And Mu'awiyah asks: if these kill those and those kill these, who will be left to look after the people, their families, their affairs? So he sends two men to Hasan, to talk.
Hasan listens, and agrees to step aside and make peace. The histories report conditions in the treaty and differ about the details, so the details are best left to them.
Bukhari's narrator ties the outcome straight back to the pulpit: through this son, God might make peace between two great groups.
Both groups are Muslims. That is what makes the moment heavy. After the Camel and Siffin, believers against believers, a grandson of the Prophet gives up a claim rather than add to the graves.

Muslims remember this differently, and fairly. Shia Muslims honor Hasan as the second Imam, and read the treaty as a wise and costly choice made to protect the believers when war would only have destroyed them.
Sunni Muslims honor Hasan as a member of the Prophet's household and a companion, and point to this hadith as the Prophet's own praise of what he did. Tradition calls that year the year of unity.
The story that began with Ali as caliph ends not on a battlefield, but with a treaty.

how: Muslims recall Hasan's treaty with Mu'awiyah through the hadith in Bukhari in which the Prophet calls Hasan a leader through whom God may make peace between two groups of Muslims; Shia Muslims honor Hasan as the second Imam.

o: Hasan stepping aside so two Muslim armies stopped
a truce Hasan won after defeating Mu'awiyah
the peace that ended the Battle of the Camel

s: the two groups in the hadith were Muslims and their enemies
both were groups of Muslims. that is what made the peace so heavy.
the Prophet said this from the pulpit, with Hasan beside him
Bukhari records him looking at the people, then at the boy.
Hasan's peace was won by defeating Mu'awiyah in battle
Hasan stepped aside and made a treaty instead of fighting.

games.q: you're Hasan. your armies are like mountains, and so are the ones facing you. two men arrive to talk. what do you do?
o: listen, and agree to step aside for peace.
leave the army and go home alone.
games.why: Hasan made peace. the narrator in Bukhari ties it to the Prophet's words: through him God would make peace between two great groups of Muslims.

practice: Bring to mind one standing argument where you are, quite possibly, right. Ask Mu'awiyah's question: if this goes on, who is left to look after the people in between, the kids, the team, the friends caught in the middle?
Hold the claim in an open hand, and see what it would cost to set it down.

wordCard.voice: Hasan's peace. A grandson of the Prophet who could have fought, and instead stepped aside so two groups of Muslims would stop killing each other. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a settlement or peace treaty, the word the sources use for Hasan's agreement.

carryVoice: Your line: peace between two groups. A costly choice, and remembered with love. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2704 (al-Hasan al-Basri's account; the Prophet on the pulpit: 'this son of mine is a sayyid… two great groups of Muslims')
al-Tabari, Tarikh (the treaty and its reported conditions; the year of unity)
